line:
"Marl, can you reach the longboat unseen and drag its oars up the bank, or pull its bung, so they can't flee by water?" When she gives her flat nod and slips off, I turn to Pell. "The wagon starts across at two, when the road opens, with Kit and me beside it in plain sight, and Corvin visible on the bench. Your six stay in the reeds until I raise my lantern-staff, and then they close both ends of the culvert."

I tuck the bait tube into my cloak where it will show when I move, and I keep Faerie Fire ready for the first man who steps out of the shed.

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~2:05 PM: Marl (Stealth 19) slipped the longboat's oars and pulled its bung unseen, and returned to the reeds. The wagon (Corvin on the bench, Wren and Kit beside it, bait tube showing in Wren's cloak) begins to cross as the causeway opens. Wren's Perception 6: she sees nothing yet. Six guards and Pell are in the landward reeds, waiting for her lantern-staff signal.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

Marl gives her flat nod and is gone. She crosses the creek mud on her belly, a grey shape among grey reeds. Some time later she is back at your elbow, wet to the thighs. "Oars up the bank," she says. "Bung out. It'll sit on the mud till the tide comes, and then it'll sink." Nobody on the far bank gave a shout.

You settle the rest with Pell. The six guards stay in the reeds until your lantern-staff goes up, and then they close both ends of the culvert. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak where it shows when you move. By two the last of the water has slid off the gravel and the causeway lies bare and shining, nine hundred paces to the drowned boat-shed.

The wagon rolls onto it at four minutes past two. Corvin sits upright on the bench with his hands visible, looking like a man being driven to a feast. Kit walks at the near wheel with her shield on her arm, and you ride Ember at the other, with the staff held upright and the brass lantern catching the sun. Gulls lift and settle on the flats. The wheels grind on gravel. Your Perception check as you start is a 6, and you see nothing but the boat-shed, which sits still and dark ahead.

The culvert is a few hundred paces on. You've three slots, all your Inspirations, Faerie Fire ready, and the whole trap behind you in the reeds. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

input.add_to_description: Day 15 ~12:15 PM: sent to sabotage the longboat; rolled a natural 1 Stealth (7 vs Sparrow's passive 16). Spotted at the creek mouth; she was not caught but fled back through the reeds with a crossbow bolt in her pack. The enemy know the trap may be watched.

entries.text: notebook: updated Marl Sedge

Marl gives her flat nod and slides back into the reeds, working along the ditch toward the creek mouth. You and Pell settle the rest: the wagon starts across at two when the road opens, with you and Kit beside it, Corvin on the bench in plain view, and the six guards holding in the reeds until you raise the lamp-staff. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak so it shows when you move.

The wait is long and quiet, and the sun climbs. A little after noon Marl is back, low and fast through the ditch, breathing hard. She reports in her flat voice that she was seen. A brown sleeve and a pale face rose over the boat-shed's sill when she was thirty paces from the creek mouth, and a crossbow bolt thudded into the reed beside her. She got away unhurt, and she holds up the bolt: fletched in grey, same as the Heron's Tithe's gear. She never touched the longboat.

So they know the far bank is watched, or at least that someone is out here. They may stay put, abandon the plan, or strike harder. The tide is still falling, and the causeway will open in under two hours. Pell looks at you and says nothing, leaving it to you.

You have three slots, all your Inspirations, Kit, and eight guards in the reeds. Faerie Fire is ready if the trap springs. What does Wren do?

She takes her place among the guards without another word.

It is just before two. You have three slots, all three Inspirations, Kit beside you, and the lantern-staff in your hand. Across 900 paces of wet road, the boat-shed waits, silent, with at least six men and one tall man in grey inside it. What does Wren do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

"Pull its bung and take its oars, and don't be seen doing it," you tell Marl. She gives her flat nod and slips into the reeds, and Pell takes your orders for the wagon without comment. Two o'clock, the road open, you and Kit beside the wheels, Corvin on the bench in plain sight. His six wait in the reeds for the lamp-staff to rise. You tuck the bait tube into your cloak where it shows when you move.

Marl does not come back, and she sends no signal. Her roll was a bare 11 against the boat-guard's watchfulness, which is not clearly unseen. You can't tell if she did it, was caught, or is only still working.

At three minutes past two the last of the water slides off the timber edging and the road lies bare. The wagon rolls out onto the Gannet Causeway at a walking pace, with the horses' hooves ringing on gravel and mud steaming on both sides. Gulls lift and settle. Corvin sits with his hands loose on his knees, humming something tuneless. Kit's shield is on her arm. You hold the lamp-staff upright, the way a road-priest would, and the brass lantern catches the sun.

Four hundred paces out, at the middle, the stone culvert squeezes the road to one cart-width with the channel running low on both sides. The wagon's front wheels are on it when the drowned boat-shed's door swings open and a lean figure in a brown coat steps out into the light, smiling, with a hand crossbow held low. Behind him, two pikemen spread along the far end of the causeway, and in the shed's shadow a tall shape in grey waits and does not come out.

You have three slots, three Inspirations, Kit beside you, and six guards in the reeds behind. Sparrow is about two hundred paces ahead and the wagon cannot turn. What does Wren do?

Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Fey Ancestry: You have advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic cannot put you to sleep.
Skill Versatility: You gain proficiency in two skills of your choice.

Bardic Inspiration (d6): You can inspire others through stirring words or music. To do so, you use a bonus action on your turn to choose one creature other than yourself within 60 feet of you who can hear you. That creature gains one Bardic Inspiration die, a d6. Once within the next 10 minutes, the creature can roll the die and add the number rolled to one ability check, attack roll, or saving throw it makes. The creature can wait until after it rolls the d20 before deciding to use the Bardic Inspiration die, but must decide before the GM says whether the roll succeeds or fails. Once the Bardic Inspiration die is rolled, it is lost. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time. You can use this feature a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (a minimum of once). You regain any expended uses when you finish a long rest.  Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain levels in this class. The die becomes a d8 at 5th level, a d10 at 10th level, and a d12 at 15th level. At level 2: Bardic Inspiration die d6.
Jack of All Trades: Starting at 2nd level, you can add half your proficiency bonus, rounded down, to any ability check you make that doesn't already include your proficiency bonus.

Song of Rest (d6): Beginning at 2nd level, you can use soothing music or oration to help revitalize your wounded allies during a short rest. If you or any friendly creatures who can hear your performance regain hit points at the end of the short rest by spending one or more Hit Dice, each of those creatures regains an extra 1d6 hit points.  The extra hit points increase when you reach certain levels in this class: to 1d8 at 9th level, to 1d10 at 13th level, and to 1d12 at 17th level. At level 2: extra 1d6 hit points.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

spellcasting.notes: Spells known are fixed until a level-up.
